_about: This subject's problem book (see principles/problem-books.md). books: external problem books to pick up. hard: named cross-chapter problems, stars 1-4, unlocked by a chapter (or a part, "4"). assignments: one-sitting builds. status: planned | written | keep | revise | drop. A written entry has problems/<id>.md.
intro: The hard problems are where probability gets fun: each one needs a trick you won't find by grinding. The assignments are evenings where you build a simulation and watch a theorem happen.

books.title: Introduction to Probability (Stat 110)
books.author: Joseph Blitzstein & Jessica Hwang
books.when: Alongside Parts 1–7. Its strategic-practice sets and story proofs are the closest match to this book's spine.

books.title: Fifty Challenging Problems in Probability with Solutions
books.author: Frederick Mosteller
books.when: After Part 3. Short, famous puzzles with careful solutions. Many of our hard problems are cousins of these.

books.title: Digital Dice
books.author: Paul Nahin
books.when: Any time after Part 2. Problems that are hard to solve on paper and easy to simulate. Pairs well with the assignments.

books.title: Mathematical Puzzles: A Connoisseur's Collection
books.author: Peter Winkler
books.when: For fun at any stage. The probability chapter is full of problems with one-line solutions that take a week to find.

books.title: Introduction to Probability
books.author: Dimitri Bertsekas & John Tsitsiklis
books.when: When you want more routine practice on a chapter: end-of-chapter problems with full solutions online (MIT 6.041).

books.title: An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Vol. 1
books.author: William Feller
books.when: After Part 7, for random walks, recurrence and combinatorial probability done by a master.

books.title: One Thousand Exercises in Probability
books.author: Geoffrey Grimmett & David Stirzaker
books.when: After Part 6 and through Part 8. A large bank with solutions, for when you want depth on one topic.

books.title: A Practical Guide to Quantitative Finance Interviews
books.author: Xinfeng Zhou
books.when: After Part 5, for speed: brain-teaser probability, expected values and martingale tricks under time pressure.

hard.title: The ménage problem
hard.idea: Couples around a table, nobody next to their partner. Inclusion–exclusion, plus a story proof for choosing non-adjacent seats on a circle.
hard.visual: The table with forbidden pairs lit up; P(nobody next to their partner) against n, creeping up to e⁻² far slower than the hat-check problem.

hard.title: Every face shows up
hard.idea: Roll a die n times. P(all six faces appear) by inclusion–exclusion over the missing faces; the same sum counts surjections.
hard.visual: A grid of rolls with missing faces greyed; the probability curve against n with the 50% crossing marked.

hard.title: Three people, one birthday
hard.idea: How big a room before three people probably share a birthday? There is no tidy product formula; count by how many pairs and triples there are.
hard.visual: The pairs curve and the triples curve side by side, and a calendar filling up.

hard.title: The ballot problem
hard.idea: A gets a votes, B gets b < a. P(A is strictly ahead throughout the count) = (a − b)/(a + b), by reflecting lattice paths.
hard.visual: A vote-count path and its reflection at the first touch of the axis, drawn together.

hard.title: Paths that never dip
hard.idea: Count lattice paths that stay above the diagonal (the Catalan numbers) with the same reflection trick, then meet them in brackets and trees.
hard.visual: All 14 paths for n = 4, the bad ones reflected onto paths to a shifted endpoint.

hard.title: Gambler's ruin
hard.idea: First-step analysis turns a game into a recurrence; the fair case is linear, the unfair case is exponential.
hard.visual: Sample paths bouncing between 0 and N; the ruin probability against starting wealth for several p.

hard.title: Penney's game
hard.idea: Pick a pattern of three coin flips; I pick mine after seeing yours, and I win most of the time. Non-transitive odds from first-step analysis.
hard.visual: A race between two patterns in a stream of flips; the 8×8 table of who beats whom.

hard.title: The boy born on a Tuesday
hard.idea: Adding an irrelevant-sounding fact changes the answer: condition on exactly what you were told, and on how you were told it.
hard.visual: The 14 × 14 grid of (child 1, child 2) with the conditioning event shaded.
hard.source: Gary Foshee (2010), after the two-child problem

hard.title: Monty Hall, three ways wrong
hard.idea: n doors; a host who opens a door at random and happens to show a goat; a host who prefers some doors. Which versions still say 'switch'?
hard.visual: A probability tree that redraws as you change the host's rule.

hard.title: Collecting every sticker
hard.idea: The expected number of packs is n·H(n) by splitting into geometric waits; the variance and the tail need the same split.
hard.visual: A sticker album filling up; the histogram of finishing times with mean ± sd.

hard.title: Banach's matchboxes
hard.idea: Two boxes of N matches, pick one at random each time. When one is found empty, how many are left in the other? A negative binomial in disguise.
hard.visual: The two boxes emptying as a random walk; the distribution of matches left.

hard.title: Waiting for HHH or HTH
hard.idea: Both patterns are equally likely in any three flips, yet you wait 14 flips on average for HHH and only 10 for HTH. Overlap is the reason.
hard.visual: A state machine that lights up as flips stream in; the two waiting-time histograms.

hard.title: The St. Petersburg paradox
hard.idea: A game with infinite expected payout that nobody would pay much to play. What expectation hides, and what utility and bankrolls change.
hard.visual: The running average payout over many games, never settling.

hard.title: The broken stick
hard.idea: Break a stick at two random points. P(the pieces form a triangle) = 1/4, read off as an area in a triangle of all possible breaks.
hard.visual: The simplex of breaks with the good region shaded; darts landing in it.

hard.title: Buffon's needle
hard.idea: Drop needles on lined paper; the crossing rate gives π. An integral over angle, or a slick linearity argument with a noodle.
hard.visual: Needles falling, crossings counted, the running estimate of π.

hard.title: Bertrand's chord paradox
hard.idea: P(a random chord is longer than the triangle's side) is 1/3, 1/2 or 1/4 depending on what 'random' means.
hard.visual: Three chord generators side by side, each filling the circle differently.

hard.title: All in one semicircle
hard.idea: n random points on a circle: P(they all fit in some semicircle) = n/2ⁿ⁻¹, by choosing which point leads.
hard.visual: Points on a circle with the covering semicircle swept round; the answer against n.

hard.title: Why your bus is always late
hard.idea: You arrive at a random time and land in a long gap more often than a short one: size-biased sampling and the inspection paradox.
hard.visual: A timeline of buses with arrival darts; the gap you land in versus the average gap.

hard.title: Adding uniforms until you pass 1
hard.idea: Keep adding Uniform(0,1) numbers until the sum exceeds 1. The expected count is e, via the volume of a simplex.
hard.visual: Sums climbing past 1; the running average of the count heading to e.

hard.title: The two envelopes
hard.idea: Switching seems to gain 25% whatever you see. The flaw is a prior that can't exist; with a proper prior the paradox dissolves.
hard.visual: The expected gain from switching, given what you see, under a few proper priors.

hard.title: The secretary problem
hard.idea: Interview n candidates, decide on the spot. Skip the first n/e, then take the next best-so-far, and you win with probability about 1/e.
hard.visual: Win probability against the cutoff, with the optimum marked as n grows.

hard.title: How many people for a ±3% poll?
hard.idea: Chebyshev says thousands, the CLT says about a thousand, Hoeffding gives a guarantee. Three bounds, three philosophies.
hard.visual: Sample size needed against margin, one curve per bound.

hard.title: The ABRACADABRA monkey
hard.idea: A monkey types random letters. The expected wait for ABRACADABRA is 26¹¹ + 26⁴ + 26, from a casino of fair gamblers and optional stopping.
hard.visual: Gamblers joining at every keystroke, their bets riding on the pattern.

hard.title: Pólya's urn
hard.idea: Draw a ball, put it back with a copy. The red fraction converges, but to a uniformly random limit: a martingale with a surprise.
hard.visual: Many urn paths fanning out and freezing; a histogram of where they end up.

hard.title: Extinction of surnames
hard.idea: Each man has a random number of sons. The family name dies out with probability equal to the smallest fixed point of a generating function.
hard.visual: Family trees growing and dying; the PGF crossing the diagonal.

hard.title: A drunk man finds his way home, a drunk bird may not
hard.idea: A simple random walk returns to the start with probability 1 in one and two dimensions, but not in three. Count returns and sum a series.
hard.visual: Walks in 1D, 2D and 3D side by side, with the fraction that have come home over time.

hard.title: PageRank by hand
hard.idea: A random surfer on a small web: the stationary distribution of a Markov chain, and why the 'teleport' makes it unique.
hard.visual: A tiny web graph with surfers flowing; ranks converging under power iteration.

hard.title: The German tank problem
hard.idea: Estimate how many tanks exist from a few serial numbers. The max is biased, and a simple correction is the best unbiased estimator.
hard.visual: Estimates from repeated samples, biased and corrected, against the truth.

hard.title: The infinite monkey theorem
hard.idea: Not just 'eventually': with probability 1 the monkey types Hamlet infinitely often. The second Borel–Cantelli lemma.
hard.visual: Expected waiting time against text length, on a log scale that runs off the chart.

assignments.title: Estimate π three ways and race them
assignments.build: Darts in a square, Buffon's needle, and the average of √(1 − U²) for uniform U, all in one script.
assignments.check: Plot the error of each against the number of samples on log–log axes; all three fall like 1/√n, at different heights.
assignments.visual: Log–log error plot with a 1/√n guide line.

assignments.title: A birthday attack on a tiny hash
assignments.build: Truncate a real hash (SHA-256) to k bits and find collisions by brute force.
assignments.check: The number of tries before the first collision grows like √(2ᵏ); fit the exponent from your own runs.
assignments.visual: Tries to first collision against k, with the √ curve overlaid.

assignments.title: Is your shuffle fair?
assignments.build: Code Fisher–Yates and the tempting wrong version (swap with any position), shuffle 3 cards a million times.
assignments.check: Fisher–Yates gives all 6 orders equally; the wrong one is visibly biased, and counting 3³ = 27 paths explains why.
assignments.visual: Bar chart of the 6 orders for both shuffles.

assignments.title: Build the medical-test explorer
assignments.build: A small page or notebook: 1,000 dots, sliders for prevalence, sensitivity and specificity.
assignments.check: At 1% prevalence and a 99%/95% test, a positive result means about a 17% chance of disease.
assignments.visual: The dot grid, coloured by true and test status.

assignments.title: A Galton board, then a wrong one
assignments.build: Simulate balls through n rows of pegs; then bias one row and make the pegs sticky.
assignments.check: The fair board matches Binomial(n, ½); the sticky one does not, and you can say which assumption broke.
assignments.visual: The histogram filling up with the binomial PMF on top.

assignments.title: Make the CLT fail
assignments.build: Average samples from uniform, exponential, Pareto with different tails, and Cauchy.
assignments.check: The first ones turn bell-shaped at different speeds; Cauchy averages never settle, because there is no mean.
assignments.visual: A grid of histograms of the average for n = 1, 5, 30, 500.

assignments.title: A Markov chain that writes
assignments.build: Train word- and character-level Markov chains on a book from Project Gutenberg and generate text.
assignments.check: Higher order gives more real words and more copying; measure how much of the output appears verbatim in the book.

assignments.title: Write a Metropolis sampler
assignments.build: Sample from a two-bump density with Metropolis–Hastings, then tune the proposal width.
assignments.check: Too small a step crawls, too large a step rejects everything; acceptance around 25–50% mixes well.
assignments.visual: Trace plots and histograms for three step sizes.
